vignette:
Arthur was sixty-seven when he finally walked into the clinic, a retired military medic who had spent decades saving lives in field hospitals and then in a civilian trauma center. The life-threatening motor vehicle collision that changed everything had happened on a Tuesday evening, three years ago. He was driving home from a late shift when a pickup truck ran a red light and smashed into his driver’s side door. The impact spun his sedan across the intersection and into a light pole; the airbag deployed with a chemical burn that he still smelled sometimes, and for a long moment he was pinned, the crumpled metal pressing against his ribs. He could hear the other driver shouting, the hiss of a ruptured radiator, and then the sharp, sweet smell of alcohol on the warm air. As a medic, Arthur had treated dozens of crash victims—but being the victim was different. In the aftermath, he found himself replaying those seconds before impact, wondering why he hadn't braked sooner, why he hadn't seen the truck coming. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted—he should have anticipated the danger, should have been more alert. That self-blame began to corrode his sense of himself; he started to doubt that he could trust his own instincts, and a quiet but persistent thought took hold: I am a weak person, I failed. That belief—that he was fundamentally unreliable—meant that things he once would have dismissed as unrelated now seemed like signs of his own failure: a car that hesitated at a green light, a stranger's impatient honk, even a discarded beer bottle on the sidewalk. That same conviction—that he should have been alert, that he had failed—kept pulling him back to the moment of impact, replaying it as though he needed to locate the exact instant he had let his guard down.

Because he believed he was weak and unreliable, Arthur began to watch his own thoughts closely, monitoring for any sign that he might be losing control or "going crazy"—a constant internal surveillance that he felt was necessary to keep himself from falling apart. The same negative appraisals also fed a chronic sense of threat: his self-doubt made him feel vulnerable in situations that had never bothered him before, and he started to experience strong physical reactions—his heart would pound, his palms would sweat—whenever something reminded him of the crash, even ordinary sounds like a car horn or the rumble of a truck. He became easily startled, and he noticed that he jumped at noises that other people didn't even register, like a door closing down the hall or the clatter of a pan in the kitchen.

The memory of the crash itself was strange to Arthur. When he tried to explain to his daughter what happened, he lost the thread halfway through, his mind going blank, and he could not finish the sentence. The memory felt alien, as though it belonged to someone else, not to him—and that feeling only deepened his self-doubt, because if the memory wasn't really his, then maybe he was losing his grip on reality. At the same time, fragments of sound would return unbidden: the screech of metal, the shouting, the hiss. These auditory recalls were often triggered by the smell of alcohol—a whiff from a passing bar or a neighbor's barbecue, and suddenly he would hear the crash again in his head. The burnt smell of an overheated engine or a toaster that had scorched a piece of bread could do the same, bringing back the chemical taste of the airbag. And when the smell triggered that memory, he would startle, his body reacting before his mind could catch up, which in turn made him even more sensitive to any new trigger—so that a car backfiring on the street would send a jolt through him, and then he would scan the air for alcohol or burnt odors, his threat system on high alert.

Arthur's attempts to manage these experiences only made things worse. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the images away whenever they surfaced, but the suppression seemed to make the memory more intrusive—it would burst into his mind at odd times, vivid and unwanted. Monitoring his thoughts for signs of craziness actually convinced him that he was weak, because the very act of checking felt like evidence that something was wrong with him. He avoided driving entirely, and he also avoided being a passenger in any vehicle, which severely limited his ability to visit his daughter or go grocery shopping; his son-in-law had to drive him to appointments, and Arthur felt a deep shame about that dependency. When he walked to the corner store, the sight of a car that had been in a minor fender bender could trigger a vivid image of his own crash, and that would make his heart race, which in turn made him look around warily for the smell of alcohol or burnt air, his threat system scanning even when he knew there was no danger. Avoiding driving kept him safe, but it also meant he spent more time alone in his apartment, where the silence sometimes gave way to auditory recalls and the feeling that the memory wasn't his. The cycle tightened: his negative appraisals made him monitor his thoughts and avoid driving; those strategies increased his physical reactivity and kept him hypervigilant; and the hypervigilance made him notice triggers more often, which brought the alien memory rushing back, which confirmed his belief that he could not trust himself. What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a moment in the grocery store: a shopper behind him smelled faintly of beer, and Arthur dropped the jar he was holding. It shattered on the floor, and he stood there trembling, unable to move, while a stranger asked if he was okay. He could not explain why he had reacted that way, and the thought that he was going crazy felt more real than ever. He came to the clinic hoping to understand what was happening to him, and terrified that the answer might be that he was simply too weak to get better.
